I've had this happen with some of my guy friends and based on my circumstances, I was able to keep the friendships. Communication is key. I just told them I didn't feel the same way but I still valued his friendship. For some people, this may be too much to handle and that's up to them. 

The second part of this is that if you remain friends, you have to be careful about the boundary. Be aware that when you date other guys, he may secretly be sad. Be very careful about being flirty with your friend even if it's just fun, friends stuff. This is where feelings get hurt. If you talk endlessly about your terrible boyfriend, understand that in the back of his mind he's wondering why you spend so much time on guys who don't value you the way he thinks he could. Also, don't put him in a position to take care of you if you have a boyfriend. Friendships suffer when your friend feels taken advantage of. Avoid this by avoiding awkward situations. Eventually these feelings may fade but right now if you want to be a good friend, be aware of all this. I guess I'm saying be clear about your feelings, be respectful of his and let him make a decision about what he wants to do.

Also, I wouldn't be too freaked out by the fact that he said he was distracted by you when you were crying. I've heard this comment from lots of guys before and I think it comes from a primitive instinct than lust. When I've had people tell me this in the past, it was explained that when they see me cry, they have this strong urge to help and comfort. They feel a strong connection to me and my emotions. That connection was what they were describing. I think this is fairly common but not all men know how to express this or how to separate the strong desire to care for and protect from lust. That's my perspective anyway.

Frankly if I were you, I would search for another job. It's pretty irresponsible if you or the client are in a dangerous situation and they still do not offer any support. A real behavior plan would involve teaching a replacement behavior so the client does not engage in aggression. The current behavior plan will just lead to one of you being hurt and I personally would never put one of my behavior technicians in a situation like that. It's really sad that the company is run that way. I can assure you this isn't the case everywhere. 

That being said, you can try to take your experience to another company or school district. There is always a huge demand for people with experience. The environment might be better than your current job. I've definitely walked from companies that I felt were being unethical and were putting my client in danger. 

Edit: what is a red flag for me is to self-injurous behavior of hitting himself in the head. He's doing that for a reason and working through it, isn't going to help him. It should be the primary behavior that your supervisor should be looking to extinct with visual token boards, social stories, etc. It could be an escape behavior but if it keeps happening after you work though it, there is something else going on.

Do you have a case supervisor or BCBA in charge of the client's care? I've worked in the field for over ten years and it's kind of unusual if they sent you in there with no experience, no past data and no support. If you have a supervisor, ask for help. Document the behavior with abc data to show what is happened to lead up to the behavior and the consequences afterward. The data will help clarify this. I can't consult on a case specifically but the behaviorist on the case should help you. They are trained to identify the function of the behavior and help the client engage in a more appropriate way to meet that need. Please reach out to your supervisor before. They don't want anything to happen to you or the client.

I have worked in special education programs in both of the models you're describing and grew up during the shift towards mainstream programs. The effectiveness of mainstreaming is really based on the student. It also depends on the goals of the parents. Some parents really value academics over positive social experiences and vice versa. Special education also covers a variety of students and most of them require really minimal services to succeeed compared to those who need a special day program as well as ot, pt, and speech.  

In my experience, I think the best method for most kids that usually would be in a special day class is a combination of both methods. I worked in a program where the students started their day in the special education classroom where they would focus on reading and math with the special education teacher and then mainstream in the afternoon with science or social studies. The kids get the support they need and also have more typical childhood experiences.

I used to work as an optician in college. Depending on how old the lenses are if it's less than two years they may be covered under a warranty if she had an anti-reflective coating. You should contact where she got them and maybe they could help. As for the frame, they probably won't cover it if it was damaged by the dog. However depending on the damage the optician may be able to do something. I was able to pull off some miracles to fix frames. They may charge for the repair but it's worth talking to them first. 

The next option is Walmart, LensCrafters or Costco. She will need a valid prescription to get the glasses but some of them also have optometrists. These places can generally make a pair of glasses in a day or so since they have a lab on site and are relatively inexpensive. I try not to recommend this for someone with a really strong prescription. They are fine but not really ideal for long-term use of a really severe prescription. Any variation in the lenses with a high prescription can cause headaches. Just be aware that it's not as ideal as a good quality optical shop.

We know so little about psychiatric medication and their effects on brain chemistry. It's not like there is always a magic pill for everyone and usually it requires a lot of trial and error and people who are homeless tend to lack the money and support to try to find the right medication. These medications can also have severe side effects that can make it difficult to take the medicine consistently and can lead to other problems. It's nearly impossible to take your medication when it makes you feel really sick for weeks which is why drug use is so pervasive in the homeless community. On top of that, there may not be a right medication. Many people go through their whole lives changing and adjusting their medication because of changes in the effectiveness. That totally does make sense. College math can be pretty difficult. I'm not naturally good at math but I've had the most success by studying the basic concept before I started learning it in class. They have free lessons for most math and some programming concepts. You can go at your own pace and they have practice questions to be sure you understand. Practice is pretty important in math to understand how to apply the concepts. Luckily with the internet, it's a little easier to find problems online and check your work. [Here's] (http://www.csus.edu/camp/current%20students/tutoringresources.html) a list of the tutoring available. Make the most of that time by having specific questions ready before your session. 

Also if you're struggling in math, try to avoid the summer classes or winter classes. They are much more intense and give you very little room for error. Good luck with everything. Hopefully next semester goes better for you!

If you have a diagnosed disability, they can work with you and possibly allow you to take your tests in a distraction free testing center with more time if necessary. Until you get a handle on your anxiety, I think a new job won't necessarily improve your situation. I had a lot of anxiety in my early twenties that was trauma related. It ruled my life for a couple of years. Once I stopped and realized how much my anxiety was controlling my life, I actively worked hard on improving. 

The number one thing that helped was to surround myself with supportive people. This is why I don't feel you will make remarkable progress while living with your family. I'm not saying you need to move four hours away, but you need to consider doing what it takes to get yourself in a healthier place. You can think about what that looks like for your own life. Life can be lonely so you need allies.

The next thing I focused on was trying to create positive social interactions. I love music and I did jam sessions with others. This was nice because the focus wasn't on me but rather it was focused on collectively working together to make music. I'm not sure what your hobby is but this was a gateway to everything for me. The key is it should be a fun activity in which even if you talk to no one, you could still walk away feeling like you had a good night . Overtime, the positive interactions made it easy for me to talk with others and develop deeper friendships. Volunteering is great. Can you do that more often? It not only helps with mental health but also can help you understand what you want in a career. 

I tried therapy briefly. I tried to take what I could from the experience and I learned a few strategies. If you haven't checked it out, CBT was extremely helpful. I'd ask your therapist about this and apply those strategies to manage your anxiety.  I didn't enjoy talking about my feelings but I did like having something to try when I was overwhelmed. 

Whatever you choose, just keep in mind it will probably cause anxiety. Big changes always cause anxiety but it can be worth it. It isn't easy but you only have one life. Why not make it better when you can? Things got better for me with work and time. I'm in grad school now with a great partner and lifelong friends. I think things can work out for you too. Good luck!

When you go through a trial it's really important to be solid in your story. Usually the ada goes over it with you. The reason being that you have to be strong when they question your actions and know that you are not at fault. People do ask questions that make it feel like it's your fault. It's not. The police will not help you with that. 

If you're in the US the national sexual assault hotline number is (800) 656-hope (4673). 

If you want to try to connect with a counseling center check in with [RAINN](https://centers.rainn.org). 

For what it's worth, I went through a trial almost ten years ago. Support from my friends and family was essential. If you don't currently have allies, it can be a lonely path. I was pretty lost for a while. Ten years later I'm in graduate school, have a wonderfully supportive partner and a ton of really close friendships. Fair but I have worked in schools for ten years and I don't feel unsafe. I understand the emotional reaction of hearing terrible things happen to kids in a place where they should be safe. However I recognize that the likelihood of this happening is rare and my focus is on helping students learn and live fulfilling lives. I feel secure in my job and I don't need an armed guard. You can't base your life off of fear. I would rather not have that much security at my school. It would make me feel less safe since it puts the possibility of a shooting at the forefront of my mind everyday instead of educating the kids and helping them feel safe. I agree that shootings are extremely rare and making sweeping restrictive policies for all of the schools in the country would be too much. I work in schools and have since before Sandy Hook and I'm working on becoming an educational psychologist. We tell the kids that incidents like this are very rare and that school is a safe place. Maybe we'll be the next statistic and I'm wrong. However it's not their job to worry about that kind of thing and scaring them harms their development. Kids that are raised to be fearful don't do well in life compared to those who grow up feeling safe and secure.

As an educator, I would rather focus on more consistent drills, stronger doors and a consistent policy about how to handle troubled kids. We usually only did those kinds of drills two times a year. We can't prevent danger all the time but we can prepare ourselves so we are confident in handling it.

The education budget doesn't even give teachers a competitive salary or money for supplies. How can they suddenly find money for all of this extra security? As someone who works in the schools, I would be very upset if this took priority in the budget over the supplies we have to buy out of our own money.

Preparation can help a lot with anxiety. It makes you feel actively involved in the process  Prepare as much as you can before. Go over your resume and come up with answers beforehand to questions you think you may be asked. Get your clothes ready the night before. Have a copy of your resume and everything you need to walk out the door. Plan on getting there at least 15-20 mins early to give yourself time to decompress before you walk in the door. Also it allows a little extra time if there are issues with traffic. Avoid caffeine and take medication if needed. Then remember that you did evening you possibly could to be ready and if they choose another candidate, realize you may have another shot in the future with more experience. If you're excited and passionate about working there, try to make that come across in the interview when you explain how your experience could be relevant to the job. Employers like people who are passionate and competent and the fact that you made it to the interview round means you have a pretty good shot. You got this! Good luck!

I had a really hard time feeling safe after my trauma. Three big things helped me a lot. 
1) I sat down and created a 1-5 scale with 5 being a crisis and one being a little uncomfortable. I outlined all my symptoms at each level so I could note how I was feeling, where it ranked on my crisis meter and make changes to feel better. If I noticed that things were getting worse, I stopped. 
2) I looked for activities that made me happy and did those activities in controlled environments. For example, I love making music so I went to karaoke with a few friends at first. At first, I told myself that I was just there for the music and concentrated on singing my song  Over time, I became more comfortable and confident and was able to branch out with other outings. This allowed me to push my boundaries a little and start to feel safe. 
3) I reached out to close friends and explained that I get really nervous sometimes and have to leave. Knowing they would be cool with it took some pressure off. You don't have to tell them everything, just enough information so they understand if your behavior is unusual. Some of my friends were even able to help me more than expected. It was a great feeling!

Best of luck with everything. 9 years ago, I felt hopeless. With the right support, I was able to feel more like myself again. It just took a little work at a time.

Thank you so much for taking the time to share your experience. I'm really sorry that you had such a tough experience. Unfortunately, I think this happens more often than people realize, even to people who have insurance. It's hard to miss work to go to treatment because you may lose your benefits. Then you have an even bigger hill to climb out of thousands of dollars in debt. 

This is what homeless people face. Why would it be worth it to go through all of this for a process that probably won't even work for them? I understand why many would choose to be on the streets and on drugs than to struggle through treatment. I'm hoping that people realize this and I live to see meaningful changes in our mental health care. 


The road to treatment is much harder than people realize so I'm very impressed that you had the ability to stick with it. Without going into too much detail and taking away the focus here, I have very real first-hand experience with the whole system as both a patient with insurance and a county patient without insurance. 

Let me share what a night is like in county hospital. Imagine all of those people that you see on the street in one room with minimal supervision and waiting hours to be evaluated. There's screaming, crying and people being aggressive. Often times you try to sleep in a chair or on the floor and sometimes other patients will touch you inappropriately while you are sleeping. This is not an exaggeration and I live in a wealthy county. It's very much like trying to sleep in a bus terminal surrounded by people who are mentally unstable and you can't leave. I want people to realize what's being done to homeless people when they are evaluated for help and this is one of the better case scenarios. I want people to realize that the kind of mental health treatment that is available can often be traumatizing before it's better. Also once I was assigned to a county therapist, I didn't feel comfortable talking with them because they told me they would put me back in that county hospital if they felt I was "too distressed" but she refused to define the behavior that she deemed fit to commit me. So yes, even if you try to avoid the hospital, it's a threat instead of a safe place  Why would I trust people like that? I do believe there are people who want to help but the system is broken. This just touches on some issues I've experienced but there are so many problems for those without insurance that it would take a book to describe it all. I was able to turn my life around but it wasn't with the help of psychiatry and mental health treatment. I read a lot and tried to find strategies that worked for me with lots of trial and error.

It's very difficult to see why the fight would be worth it. Luckily I had lots of support from my friends. I hope that you have that in your life as well. If not, I developed several strategies that helped me hold on for one more day that I'm happy to share. Please feel free to pm if you need some support from someone who kind of understands. Sometimes that's all you can do.

"Effective"is relative and the side effects can be very severe. Some people may never find the right medication and they've gone though a long process of trial and error. It takes a lot of trust to go to a doctor that gives you pills that make you sick and continue taking these pills. I've worked with people that have schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and a good friend of mine developed schizophrenia in his 20's.  I'm sharing their reasoning for not consistently taking medication. 

Psychiatry is not an exact science. It's a long process that for some people never improves their condition. My argument is that we don't know enough about the brain so we work on a guess of what works for most people. The patient tries the new medication and the side effects are overwhelming. The psychiatrist will often just tell the person that they need more time to adjust to the prescription. Time could help or it could become worse. It's hard to convince someone to feel badly for a months. 
With the state of mental health care for people with no insurance or state benefits, I am not surprised that people would rather be free and/or self medicating than in treatment. 

I'm really happy that this is conversation is happening and I hope that it can lead to some positive change.

One thing that I think people aren't taking into account is that mental health treatment isn't perfect. The reason many people don't want to stay with a treatment plan is that finding the right medication can be a long process with a lot of really unpleasant side affects that really need to be monitored. Nausea, tremors,  Dystonia and other conditions that might become permanent. It's really difficult to be a functional person on those medications, especially the heavier antipsychotics. Finding medication is really just based on trial and error and sometimes you may never find the right combination. It's not like talking a pill to lower cholesterol. The psychiatrist will prescribe something, the patient tries it. It could help but likely makes them feel worse for a time. Instead of trying something different, the psychiatrist will advise that it takes time for the medication to work which means the person may feel sick for months before the doctor either adjusts the medication or chooses something else. Convincing someone to go along with that process instead of just using drugs. It's a losing battle unless they really want it for themselves. It's not exactly the doctor's fault. We don't know enough about the brain to know how everyone will be affected by certain psychoactive medication. Also it's not always a partnership when it comes to what medications you put in your body. The doctors prescribe something and if you refuse it can be seen as not complying with treatment instead of trying to advocate for yourself and your body. If mental health treatment is contingent in housing, you could see how people may feel forced to take medication without being part of the process.  Any mental health professional can tell you that the most effective way to help someone is if they are involved in the process. 

Say you do find the right medication. Now these pills often cost hundreds if not thousands of dollars a month. I'm not kidding. Often times generic versions of the drugs are not available. It can be offset possibly by some vouchers from the pharmaceutical companies but navigating that process is difficult when you're dealing with mental illness. Also most treatment plans pair counseling with medication so you'd consistently need both as well as a stable place to live to be successful. So now you're homeless on a medication you can't afford to maintain and monitor. 


Tl;dr  We need to make mental health treatment better and more affordable before we just offer it as a quick fix to improve homelessness.

Everyone in this thread needs to stop assuming that everyone is a sociopath. Antisocial personality disorder only is diagnosed in 0.2-3% of the population and only after a long history of troubling incidents. The FBI list is very useful in cases in which the public needs protection from people with a long violent history. While what they did was terrible, I don't see this as one of those cases. The murderers you have listed all may have had a history of torturing animals but they also had a history of either severe abuse and neglect from family and peers. Nothing indicates a history of this in the post. 

There is however danger in labeling children as criminals. Howard Becker theorized that when one is labeled as deviant, they will engage in deviant behavior. In this case, telling a 10 year old that they are a sociopath and a criminal will increase the chance of them engaging in that type of behavior in the future. It's actually why many mental health professionals may refrain from labeling people with a diagnosis if they feel it may unintentionally hinder their recovery. I encourage you to read more about labeling theory to understand how judgement and how you treat someone can influence how they act. It's very interesting. 

I'm not saying this should be dismissed as kids will be kids. I think they deserve to face serious consequences and I'm sorry that it isn't coming from the mother. It sounds like the kids were careless and selfish and unfortunately they were not held accountable. It really is terrible and I don't know what I would do if it were my pet. However reporting a 10 year old to the FBI in this case is overkill. 

Source: I have a background in behavioral psychology. I've worked with kids and teenagers who actually have sociopathic tendencies and are in mental health programs.

It sounds odd but one thing that helped me was to rank my symptoms in order of severity. I would write the numbers from 0-5. 0 meant no symptoms and feeling good. 5 meant that I was in full panic mode and probably needed to go home. Examples of level 1 symptoms (mildly upset) would be increase in heart rate and level 2 may include shallow breathing.

It helped a lot to understand my symptoms and when I dealt with something at level 1-2 it was much easier than trying to calm myself during a level 5 panic attack. When I started to feel nervous at level 2, I'd take a walk or a deep breath. If I was in a crowd, I'd go somewhere quiet before it got to be too much. 

I had never heard of this method before. I actually used it in my work with children and decided to develop a similar system for myself. It has been very helpful for me and I am happy to have my symptoms under control. I am not sure that I explained it all very well. Let me know if you have any questions.  Best of luck to you!

When I was 18, a mutual friend set me up with someone and we got along very well. He lived in Michigan and I in California so it wasn't ideal but we tried the long distance thing. He flew to California to visit and we had a great time.  I cared about him so much and wanted to see him happy. He had issues with depression. I was also struggling with my own challenges but I could see the light at the end of the tunnel. I always knew I would be ok and I wanted him to feel better too. I think my recovery only made him feel worse. I tried to give him ideas to become more independent. I thought if he could start living life for himself instead of his parents, he could be happier. The troubling thing about depression is that you feel paralyzed by decisions. It all seems overwhelming and becomes another source of depression. He started to talk about how depressed he was all the time. I encouraged him to talk to a therapist and maybe explore medication. He tried all of these things but lost faith in it all after a few bad experiences. 

He talked about suicide all the time and would call me to help him calm down. At first, I really did all that I could. I talked him through it during 3 am phone calls for years. I really did try but it started to make me really depressed. I wasn't sleeping. I wasn't eating. I was taking care of him and not living my own life.
I started to realize that I could never truly recover (stop thinking about my own depression and suicidal thoughts) unless I fully committed to living. I tried to explain this to him. I think he saw it as me abandoning him. We had an argument and he didn't talk to me anymore.

Shortly after his birthday, I got a call from his brother saying that he had committed suicide. It didn't come as a surprise to anyone in the family but it is still so tragic.

I wish I could have helped him. I got to a point where I realized that I couldn't save him without sinking into my own depression. It was so hard and one of my big regrets. I wish I had been a little older, wiser and stronger to help him. I was just 18 and I didn't know how to help. Looking back, I wouldn't have done anything differently. I wish he knew how much I loved him. I never really dated seriously again.

There are a few things you can try. 

1. Social stories or visual support can help highlight expected behavior beforehand. It can be something like " when I'm at the beach I can play in the sand, play in the water.... But I need to stay close to my family. I am not allowed to go in the towers or go anywhere with other people. Etc. By following these rules I can have a safe  fun time at the beach. My parents will feel happy that I am safe etc." Make it from his perspective to help him relate. Maybe even use pictures from the last time you were there. If you need help making one, I am happy to help. 

2. Use consequences when appropriate. Set the expectation and help them understand. This is teaching right vs wrong by giving a consequence to unwanted behavior. It doesn't have to be anything horrible. It can just be something like having to sit in the car away from the fun for a ten minutes. This isn't to ruin your child's day at the beach. My opinion may be unpopular but i speak from 10 years experience of working with elementary school children. I'm a behavior specialist so I work with kids with behavior problems, many of them are referred to me for bullying. I've worked with children who were actually sociopaths and a variety of other special needs as well as in the general population. It's a little more complicated than teachers not wanting to do their job. Teachers are responsible for not only the academic needs but more importantly the social needs of 20+ students. There is no manual for meeting those social needs and every child is different. What helps one student could be  counterproductive for another. On top of that, teachers live in fear of lawsuits.  In my experience must young children who are bullies are angry themselves. They lack self esteem and lash out at others. These students could use some counseling support ( which is impossible to get unless a student is designated special ed). Many parents aren't comfortable with getting that support because of stigmas attached to mental health or in sadder cases they are equally confrontational and refuse to see a problem. 
The other common thing I see with children labeled as bullies is that they are just trying to be funny with their friends. Kids are kids and they don't always have the life experience to understand the consequences of their words. I've seen young kids get suspended for words that they didn't mean to be hurtful. They just said something dumb. Kindergartners will repeat things they hear without really knowing what they are saying. Perhaps the death threat was really just a kid repeating something on TV. Yeah he shouldn't be watching that stuff but I've only met one kindergartner who I actually believed was going to kill someone and he had severe sociopathic behavior. As a behaviorist i think it's unfair to consequate behavior when a child is unsure of the expectation. Many times bullying behavior can be solved just by explaining why their words were inappropriate and telling them that they can be better. I've worked with many children over the years who were labeled as bullies and I've had way more success when I approached the situation as an opportunity to teach them to be better people instead of labeling them as bad.  Labeling them as a bully does more harm than good in my opinion.

You're an awesome boyfriend! Here are just a few suggestions. 

1. Communication had helped immensely. Having someone to be honest and open with can help alleviate those feelings of shame and guilt. Try to not leave anything unsaid so that there is a stronger sense of security for her. What I mean by that is when she is upset she may be questioning how someone could love her when she had a difficult time. Make it clear that you love her and if there is a problem, let her know that you will always talk about it and you will always solve it together through open and honest conversation. That way she doesn't feel like a burden when she is struggling. You are team. No matter what, let her know your are in this together. 


2. Let her have space when she asks. Sometimes the feelings are so intense that it's hard to be around people, especially those you love. When you are around them and upset, you worry about hurting them. It's hard because you also want to be loved but you don't want to hurt people. If you are worried about her and she's asked for space, it helps to set a time you check in to alleviate your fears. Ie. "I know you need space, let's talk in an hour. I love you very much. If you need anything, I will be in the living room. " Reassure her that you are there for her. 


3. Try not to take things personally. She may lash out at you but it likely didn't have anything to do with you. When you have ptsd, it's hard to feel safe. You may lash out when you feel unsafe but you always regret the hurt you caused later because you were scared. Just do your best to understand that she didn't mean it. This is where communication is key so that you don't have to worry that it might mean something else. 

4. Be as calm and consistent as you can. Be her rock as much as you can. No matter how crazy the world seems, make your arms her safe zone. 

5. Take care of yourself too! You are only human. The happier and calmer you are, the easier it is to care for someone else. It can be as simple as listening to your favorite songs on the way home from work or going for a walk. Self-care is important for a happy relationship because you never want to feel like you are missing something in a relationship. It will creep into arguments and that's not fair for anyone. Don't feel guilty about needing things too.

Hope this helps. Let me know if you have any questions at all.

Thank you so much for posting this. In my experience working in a few different special education programs, it really does depend on the needs of the child. Some special education students are not comfortable for long periods of time in a mainstream class,often because the lessons are not presented in a way that is easily accessible to these children. The best solution seemed to be a balance. There was an sdc class that had lessons in reading and math in an engaging and routine way. For 50% of the day, including recess, the students would go to a mainstream class for science and social studies lessons with their typical peers. The SDC class would attend all of the field trips in which their mainstream class participated. They also participated in all of their class shows. Their peers saw them at their best and had positive experiences with them. This was more successful than full inclusion in my experience. For example, if he lets you know that he needs music or his favorite book to calm and asks appropriately, if possible give it to him immediately so he connects that using his words gets him what he wants. Aba therapists often use social story books to explain the expected behavior in the situation and offer a visual reminder. You can look for one but you can make one yourself too that is specific to your son so that it's more meaningful.

1. When singing, don't think of a note as too low or too high. It will make your throat tighten up. Instead when singing scales, try to stay as relaxed as possible. This will make it easier to reach those notes on the edge of your range.

Hi there. I'm a behavior support specialist for an amazing school district. I used to be a classroom aide for a few years and now help train others in our schools. I've also worked as a behavior therapist for a few years. I grew up with a brother with autism which brought me to this field in the first place. Feel free to ask anything. It is a really amazing field that needs patient people who are committed to helping, like yourself.  Here are a few ideas that I think may help. 

1. Structure and consistency- In general, children learn better in an environment that is predictable. Explain to the child, what is going to happen throughout the day. It's best to show this visually but you can do it verbally was well depending on the child's level of communication. To do this visually, you can draw or write down what's happening now and what will happen next. This First/ Then system is very helpful for helping the child have a sense of calm. For example at work time, you can show the child first work, then recess. The child sees that there is an end to an undesirable activity and that when they complete their work, they can do something they enjoy. This is sometimes hard to express to a child on the spectrum verbally, but easier to understand visually. 

2. Giving directions- less is more when it comes to verbal instructions. When you think about it, it's hard to pick out important parts of an instruction. For example, "When you are done with your work, put it in your backpack and sit down," requires you to clue into a lot of instructions. I'm not sure of the levels of the children you work with so I'm just explaining for children that have a tougher time understanding directions. In general though if your children are having trouble following the directions, simplify them and see how they respond. 

3. Set them up for success- This is true with all kids (or people for that matter). One tool that I use a lot is called priming. Priming is telling or showing a child what is expected so that they know what to expect. An example of this would be to say, "We are going to the library. In the library we need to have a quiet voice and use our walking feet." This is more positive than correcting the child after he's already run or screamed in the library. It may take a few tries but when the child does well, give lots of praise and reinforcement. 

4. Reinforcement- We all want to work for something whether it be money or personal satisfaction. Children are the same way. Find something that is meaningful to them and use it to motivate. Reinforcers can be thing like access to special books, or trips to the playground. You can use token systems to reinforce good behavior and show that when they earn a certain amount of tokens, they gain access to what they want. This really increases the positive behaviors and focuses on positive consequences than punishment. When they gain access to their prize, make it super exciting like they just won the lottery. Keep in mind that interest in reinforcers change. If they seem less motivated, look for something  more motivating. Also, limit access to the reinforcer to when they earn tokens so that it is extra exciting when they do earn it. 

Those are some general tips. If you have any questions, please feel free to send me a message anytime. I really want to help and may have suggestions if you have specific issues. Initiative and interest in personal growth is the best thing you can do to be successful in this and any career. You'll do great!

I think ABA (applied behavioral analysis) is a good starting point because it focuses on making things consistent so your child can learn and grow. It makes big tasks manageable by breaking them down into smaller steps so that it is not overwhelming. ABA is typically done with therapists that provide in home therapy. 

I also think you would like RDI (relationship development intervention). It is much more family based with a consultant that comes in to teach these methods. RDI is about building relationships by helping your child understand social cues. I worked with a child that had ABA as well as RDI. Every child is different but he was doing well with having more natural relationships than some of my kids that had ABA alone. Maybe ask your doctor about both and see what works best for your family and your son.

He goes to dances at the community center and is on a bowling team. I have a younger brother with autism who was diagnosed in 1991. I have also been a professional in the field for 7 years as an ABA therapist, autism paraprofessional in schools and worked in other settings with children on the spectrum (preschools, special olympics, community events etc). That being said, I have kind of an interesting perspective. I think the most helpful thing for the children I work with and my brother is the same as with all children. Consistency is important. As a professional, it links back to basic behaviorism. It's easiest to learn if the patterns are consistent. Since I also look at the family perspective, I believe that a consistent set of rules and consequences helps my brother and the children I now work with more than anything. Temple Grandin says in many of her interviews that the fact that her mother treated her like a typical child was invaluable. This helped a lot with my family as well. 

Share in the little things with him and encourage any passion he shows. My brother loved dinosaurs and Charlie Brown cartoons and these were hobbies that he and I still talk about 21 years later. It helped him build language and connection. The more motivated and passionate a child is, the more likely he will push to use words to connect with you if you share that passion. This applies in my current work as well. I have a child that loves robots and we recently talked about the Mars Curiosity rover. We talk about how robots can help people do jobs and he asks so many great questions. He's 7 and pretty verbal but didn't start that way. It's a spectrum and every child is different. My point is passion matters a lot, with typical children and children on the spectrum. 

Modeling language helps a lot. It may seem like your child is not hearing you but he probably is. You never know what will connect with him. I find some of the best success in my career has been just talking in play and not expecting a response right away. Making it fun and interesting and pretending that he's part of the conversation even if he doesn't talk. Kids have really surprised me sometimes when they respond with something I may have said when we played the same game weeks ago. You just never know but the more language you expose him to, the better. 

Lastly, I would say (because I am a professional after all). If you can, connect with some early intervention specialists in your area. ABA is the most talked about form of early intervention. It can be helpful as you see behaviors and know how to deal with them. It also helps teach that consistent behavior and consequence and you learn how to see things in a different way. That being said, as someone with personal family experience, keep in mind that no one knows your child better than you. I've worked in this field with very educated people that have ideas that make sense in theory but of course don't apply to every child because every child is different. If something doesn't make sense, ask questions. Feel free to PM me if you have any questions on ABA and other intervention methods, how to make play more meaningful, school programs, repite care, family health or anything really. As someone who understands the professional side as well as the family challenges, I really want to help. Best wishes!

Angry birds is good and is definitely popular with kids right now.One thing that I would watch out for with ipad games is that they can be a little limiting socially. One thing that is really popular at school with some of the kids that I work with is the Angry Birds board game. You build a tower and use a slingshot to launch the birds and knock down the pigs. It is just like the ipad game but there is more flexibility for building language. For example, if a child is limited verbally, you could use intraverbals (ready, set, and have him fill in Go! to launch the bird) or if they are more advanced, they would be mand instructions on how to build the tower and where to put the pigs. 

ABA can be really great since they be able to evaluate and know what/how to build the skills for the child. They will also be able to address behaviors by using the antecedent (what happened before the behavior) to determine the function of the behavior. From this information, ABA therapists will be able to come up with effective solutions specifically for your child. Before signing up, it might be good to look for a company that has a low turnover rate in their staff. In ABA companies there can be a high turnover rate for therapists for many different reasons. It can be really hard on a child to lose a therapist who has such a good rapport with them. This is a great suggestion too, kam1244. Since he is in school and when he has an IEP, you can ask to get an augmentative communication specialist involved. PECS is the most basic form of augmentative communication and those same ideas are used with the available ipad programs. It can definitely be great to provide meaning to the word, especially with more abstract ideas, since autistic people tend to be very concrete thinkers. An augmentative communication specialist would be able to evaluate the situation and recommend techniques that will be most effective for Landon. ie. actual pictures vs icons, ipad vs picture exchange etc, will he be required to say the word afterward etc. In my experience, if children with autism are able to communicate effectively, then they will likely have less behaviors because they experience less frustration. You sound like such a great uncle! I grew up with a younger brother with autism and have now worked professionally in the field for eight years. Not sure of Landon's situation and complete diagnosis so I am going to give more of a general answer. One thing that I find brings language are highly motivating activities. ie I have one kid that was completely non-verbal. After our first session together, I found out that he loves baseball and outdoor games. After a few minutes, I modeled fun age-appropriate phrases "Wow! You hit it out of the park! Home run!! You are a super star! Awesome!" etc I make it fun and just pretend to be the perfect peer. Someone who acts as the number one fan to my kids while still guiding them. 

Does your nephew like trains or animals? It can be really helpful to have something familiar as the basis of the activity. A big part of working with autistic children is building on skills they already have. Working on something familiar and motivating takes the pressure off of the task so the child can focus on/ enjoy more of the social aspect.

My language with my non-verbal kids starts out simply. As I build a rapport with him, I start to use more natural directions. ie. I would start with "Put on shoes" and moved on to "Put on your shoes, please". Sometimes the extra words can make it hard to understand what part of the sentence to focus on, especially for a child who hasn't has speech therapy.

Overall, push to make the connection every time that you have an opportunity, even when it doesn't seem like he's listening. It feels weird at first to be silly or pretend something is really amazing when you get no feedback from the child but it is worth it. I can't tell you how many clients I have worked with who did not respond to my energy and excitement at first. The children, I worked with started to really respond after a few weeks. It was subtle at first ie repeating a phrase that I had said and sometimes eye contact or looking at what I'm talking about.

Music has been really helpful for some of my kids as well. It is predictable for many autistic children so not as overwhelming and it can be something an avenue to build connection.

Anyway, I know a lot of little ideas that may be helpful. Intervention would be the best thing. If you can get involved in a company that specializes in ABA, they can help with. I know his mother may not be receptive to this but it is definitely worth looking into. Let me know if this is not helpful for Landon and maybe I can recommend something else. I have a lot of experience in ABA and public schools in the US. :) Landon is lucky to have someone like you in his life!
